# The Advocacy of Democratic Governance by India and China: Patterns of Consistency/Inconsistency between Declaratory and Operational Practices

Andrew F. Cooper 1,2 Asif B. Farooq 3,4

## Abstract

This article examines the patterns of consistency and inconsistency between how India and China advocate democratisation at the global and national levels. Addressing this question through a dualis tic framework, we develop a detailed map of the rhetorical promotion of democratic governance by India and China through an analysis of 10 years of foreign affairs speeches, remarks, interviews and statements of political elites of both countries. The article argues that although China has not shied away from declarations on democracy domestically as well as on global governance, the contradictions between the clear and consistent push for democracy and equity at the global level and the highly contingent commitment to democracy at the national level remain highly salient. India’s deficiencies, by way of contrast, come not in the domain of legitimacy but effectiveness. India’s struggle to trans late its domestic democratic credibility into more equitable representation at the global institutional level and into a stellar economic model at the domestic level exposes it to criticism in relationship to China. Yet, even with these gaps, the article concludes that India has some comparative advantages over China precisely because it can play a consistent two-level game in terms of the promotion of democracy both at global and state levels.

Keywords India, China, democracy promotion, Chinese characteristic, Chinese model, democracy fund

## Introduction

Comparisons between India and China both in terms of their domestic political and economic develop ment and their emerging global roles are highly compelling. India is the world’s largest democracy with the highest number of people living in abject poverty; yet, it prefers to pursue economic growth without compromising democratic principles. China has an extremely impressive recent record of eco nomic performance, alleviating almost 600 million out of poverty, but is one of the longest surviving one-party states. Unlike India, China places development, harmony and cohesion above democratic values. Their enhanced economic weight has enabled both India and China to expand their global voice and influence, but gaps in research exist about the patterns of consistency and inconsistency between how these two countries advocate democratisation of global governance and the promotion of democracy at the state level. Both China and India contend that the institutional architecture of global governance is misaligned, with the levers of power still held by the traditional establishments in the North. Greater equality is advocated by both countries on grounds of fairness as well as in terms of the rationale of problem solving, be that in international financial institutions (IFIs), the Group of 20 (G20) or in the World Trade Organization (WTO). Yet, this parallelism of purpose is splintered by nuanced individual differences between the positions of China and India. China’s arguments for greater equality in the global system have been targeted towards the IFIs. India’s calls for the shape shifting of global institutions is, in com parison, more ambitious and challenging in that the centrepiece of its campaign highlights the need for reform of the United Nations Security Council (UNSC). China’s arguments downplaying universal conceptions of democratic values in favour of the instru mental benefits of its model of economic development at the state level also have considerable attractions. Nonetheless, the contradictions between the clear and consistent push for democratisation at the global level of governance and the highly contingent commitment to democracy at the national level jump out. These deficiencies are reinforced over time by the fact that China’s own model is con tested, with at least some scholars mooting the inevitability of China’s transformation into a democracy (Rowen 1996; Gilley 2004). India’s deficiencies come not in the domain of legitimacy but effectiveness, as Pattnayak (2007, 79) quotes Edward Luce, ‘India is not an autopilot to greatness, but it would take an incompetent pilot to crash the plane’. At the domestic level, India’s failure to translate its democratic credibility into a stellar economic model of poverty reduction exposes it to comparative criticism with respect to China. Yet, it can be suggested that India has some comparative advantages over China precisely because it can play a consistent two-level game in terms of adhering to the principles of democratic governance both at global and state levels. Pushing for democratic reform of the global order is validated by India’s strong record of democratic practices at home and its growing willingness to promote democracy at the state level. In teasing out these analyses, we develop a detailed discursive map of India and China’s promotion of democratic governance both at the global institutional level and at the national or state level. In the first section of this article, we examine how the political elites of both countries articulate their coun tries’ position with regard to democracy. We examine foreign affairs speeches, remarks and statements of the Indian and Chinese political elites from 2004 to 2013 by using qualitative content analysis. Our comparative analysis, on the one hand, contributes to a broader understanding of emerging powers’ declaratory practice in constructing social reality about them in international relations. It also reveals how China, despite being a one-party state, does not shy away from referring to democracy and co-opts it to its Chinese characteristics. On the other hand, it adds value to the international relations literature by identifying the sources of consistency/inconsistency that intersect international and domestic politics.

Catwright (2009) made a similar analysis, although in a more limited manner, with an exclusive focus on India’s prime minister’s (PM) speech from 2004 to 2007. Our article is more extensive, with a com parative analysis of 10 years of foreign affairs speeches, remarks and statements made by the political elites of India and China from 2004 to 2013. We used 1,891 sample speeches in total for the content analysis, where 1,386 of them belong to India and 505 of them belong to China. 1 Our objective is to make a qualitative comparative assessment of how the political elites of both countries express democracy in public declarations, and provide an explanation of the rationale behind the contrasting discursive approaches. Foreign policy discourses or speech construct social realities, often reinforcing a binary world, such as democratic/authoritarian, equitable/unjust and North/South (Derrida 1981), and operationalise a ‘regime of truth’ that produces a specific mode of identity and action through declaratory practices (Milliken 1999, 229–231). Finlayson and Martin (2008, 450) also contend: [t]he political speech is an argument of some kind: an attempt to provide others with reasons for thinking, feeling or acting in some particular way; to motivate them. To invite them to trust one in uncertain conditions; to get them to see situations in a certain light. Apposite to our specific research project, Yang (2007) argued how reviews of speeches by the President Hu Jintao and Premier Wen Jiabao illustrate China’s ruling elites’ discourse on democracy. Similarly, the Indian foreign secretary stressed how important it is for Indian diplomats to advocate and explain to the world the Indian ‘brand’, with the ‘compelling narrative surrounding the largest democracy’, which is often captured in Indian political elites’ foreign affairs speeches, remarks and statements. Therefore, content analysis of foreign affairs speeches of the Indian and Chinese political elites can provide con structive references to their ideological and institutional positions about their countries’ policy on democracy promotion. In the final sections, we elaborate on the trajectory and implications of both countries’ two-level games on democracy, with a focus on the approaches taken by India and China in terms of the democra tisation of global institutions and the promotion of national or state-based models of democracy in declaratory statements and operational practice. To put it simply, we analyse the logic of motivations and results in possessing consistency or inconsistency in the two-level games.

Promoting Democratic Governance: India versus China The conceptual stance of India and China on the promotion of democratic governance converges on global institutional level. However, a differentiated ideological approach underpins their position on state-level promotion of democratic governance. Adhering to their historical, stronger stance on the sanctity of sovereignty and non-intervention, both countries emphasise every state’s ‘equality’ on its right to self-determinism in international relations. Nonetheless, their ideological solution to global institution’s ‘democracy deficit’ is not equality per se, rather what is ‘equitable’. On the one hand, although the rhetorical currency of promoting democratic governance is founded on fair representation of the South in global institutions, often mobilised under the converging interests of the South–South solidarity, both India and China will be the chief beneficiaries from institutional reform on global level given their disproportionate weight based on the size of economy compared to their Southern partners. Thus, India and China converge on the conceptual notion of democracy based on equity on global institutional level. On the other hand, both countries take a differentiated conceptual stance about democratic governance on state level. India’s conception of democracy in practice corresponds to Dahlian (Dahl 1971) procedural democracy (given its track record of electoral continuity) or to Marshall’s (1964) citizenship democracy (given its inclusive constitution, affirmative action and welfare pro gramme on food security). In contrast, China co-opted the term ‘democracy’ into its Chinese character istics and has not shied away from taking a strong rhetorical stance defending it. Nevertheless, there is a deep division on the conceptual clarity of democracy with Chinese characteristics among Chinese schol ars, which we elaborate later in our analysis. In terms of motivations, Indian and Chinese political elites aim to strategically lever declaratory references with respect to democracy in their speeches of foreign affairs.
